evaluated.name: Unjustified-Discount Gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(MA(RATIO(ib, at), 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within an industry, the part of a firm's cheapness that is not matched by its distress ranking is mispricing; the part that is matched is fair compensation for default risk.
evaluated.reasoning: Differencing the industry rank of book-to-market against the industry rank of a fundamental distress score (leverage plus smoothed three-year profitability) yields an explicit residual-discount measure, so the signal is large only when a firm is cheap without a distress justification. Industry ranking removes sector-level leverage norms and multiple levels that would otherwise drive the spread.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Weakest-Link Cheap and Debt-Serviceable
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dlc), lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value premium is conjunctive rather than additive: a firm must be both cheap and able to cover its liabilities out of internally generated cash after current maturities, and failing either condition destroys the premium entirely rather than partially offsetting it.
evaluated.reasoning: MIN replaces the fixed-weight rank blend with a non-substitutable (Leontief) interaction, so a very high book-to-market can no longer compensate for weak debt-service capacity the way it does in a Piotroski-style additive score. The distress channel is a flow-versus-stock coverage measure, (oancf - dlc)/lt, rather than a leverage level, and firms with negative book equity or negative post-maturity cash flow are correctly pinned to the short leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Within-Cheap Health Dispersion
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(oancf, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: All of the economically interesting variation lies inside the cheap segment: among value stocks, those with accumulated retained earnings and cash-flow coverage of liabilities are compensated value, while those without are distress traps, and non-cheap firms carry no directional information at all.
evaluated.reasoning: The gate is now placed on the valuation dimension, not the distress dimension, so the ranked variable driving the sort is a continuous health z-score measured only where the value story applies; the zero block is genuinely neutral (non-cheap firms) instead of dumping distressed names into the middle alongside healthy glamour firms. Both extreme legs are therefore populated exclusively by cheap firms sorted by solvency, which is a direct test of the healthy-versus-trap split rather than a restatement of a screened value strategy.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap Intensity
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5), RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Lottery-like distress traps are firms whose price is low relative to sales precisely because they have repeatedly lost money and carry net debt they cannot retire; investors overpay for the small recovery option, so trap intensity predicts underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: Cheapness is measured with sales-to-price, whose numerator and denominator are both positive, eliminating the negative-book-equity sign inversion that made the earlier version place the most distressed firms on the long leg. Distress severity is continuous and multi-year, blending the count of loss years over five years with net-debt-to-assets, so the sort has no degenerate mass of zeros and the product is maximal only for the cheap-and-chronically-impaired intersection.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash-Runway Value Trap
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, what predicts underperformance is not leverage per se but the absence of a near-term cash runway: cheap firms holding little cash against current liabilities must sell assets or issue equity at depressed prices, transferring value away from shareholders.
evaluated.reasoning: This deliberately strips out every solvency and profitability input so that the interaction rests on one clean liquidity channel, letting us attribute the trap alpha to funding capacity rather than to earnings quality already spanned by RMW. If it reproduces the trap alpha with no profitability ingredient, the mechanism is refinancing pressure; if it fails, the earlier alpha was a profitability effect in disguise.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Repaired-Balance-Sheet Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(lt, at), 5), RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose leverage now sits far below its own five-year peak have completed a balance-sheet repair that removed the default risk originally responsible for the discount, but the discount persists because investors anchor on the prior distressed state.
evaluated.reasoning: Distance from a firm's own leverage maximum is a within-firm recovery measure that is not a cross-sectional quality score, so it should not be absorbed by RMW or CMA the way the failed healthy-cheapness composites were. This is the constructive counterpart to the trap signals: it asks whether the positive polarity can work at all once the healthy leg is defined by distress *resolution* rather than by static financial strength.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-History Distress Spiral
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is in a spiral when it is simultaneously at the cheapest point of its own valuation history and the most indebted point of its own balance-sheet history; this joint own-history extreme signals an ongoing deterioration that cross-sectional levels miss for firms that are permanently cheap or permanently levered.
evaluated.reasoning: Cross-sectional cheapness and leverage ranks are dominated by stable industry and business-model differences, whereas own-history positioning identifies firms actively moving into distress, which is a distinguishable economic mechanism rather than a rescaling of Signal 1. Because both legs contain firms at varying cross-sectional cheapness levels, the spread should carry small net HML exposure and hence be harder for FF5 to explain.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Trade-Credit-Squeezed Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose liability stack is dominated by non-debt claims (payables, accruals, pension and other operating obligations) rather than negotiated debt are squeezed by suppliers and counterparties who can withdraw credit without a restructuring process, so their apparent earnings cheapness accrues to those claimants rather than to shareholders.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the archive's net-debt/leverage channel entirely and replaces it with the composition of liabilities, a distinct distress mechanism: non-debt obligations carry no covenant renegotiation option, so operating creditors impose discipline exactly when the equity is already cheap. Pairing it with EBITDA-to-market rather than sales-to-market also changes the valuation leg to a margin-sensitive multiple, so the test is not a one-ingredient substitution into Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Twin Deterioration
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(pi, at), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: For firms already trading at low multiples, the market underreacts to the joint direction of change in solvency and profitability: rising liabilities alongside falling pretax income confirms that the discount reflects genuine deterioration rather than temporary pessimism.
evaluated.reasoning: Both deterioration channels now move the same way with distress — a rise in liabilities-to-assets and a decline in pretax return on assets — removing the earlier accrual-anomaly sign conflict from the working-capital leg. Pretax income is used so the profitability trajectory is not contaminated by tax-benefit recognition, which is itself mechanically linked to distress.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payout-Coverage Mismatch Trap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(pi, txt), lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is a value signal only when earnings comfortably cover near-term obligations; firms distributing cash while after-tax income is small relative to current liabilities are financing payout from a shrinking buffer, and the eventual dividend cut triggers a repricing and yield-investor exit.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops market leverage and market-scaled income entirely, so it no longer reproduces the Campbell-Hilscher-Szilagyi or Bhandari inputs; the distress leg is an accounting coverage ratio of after-tax earnings against current liabilities, and the valuation leg is the payout-based cheapness channel untested elsewhere in the archive. The interaction is genuinely conditional in economics: identical yields carry opposite information depending on whether the payout is covered, which is why the product form, not either leg alone, should predict returns.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Unstable Fundamentals
evaluated.hypothesis: The lottery half of the economic story is about the *variance* of fundamentals, not their level: a cheap firm whose pretax return on assets swings widely has an equity claim resembling an out-of-the-money option, and investors overpay for that skewness.
evaluated.reasoning: Every distress measure tested so far is a first-moment level or change; five-year volatility of pretax profitability is a second-moment channel that formalizes "lottery-like" without using leverage or losses at all. If this reproduces the trap alpha, the effect is about payoff convexity rather than solvency, which would substantially redirect the remaining search.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Low Recovery Value
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes cheapness dangerous is not the size of the claims but what shareholders would recover: a cheap firm whose assets are overwhelmingly illiquid and long-lived cannot raise cash without fire-sale discounts, so operating earnings never reach equity holders.
evaluated.reasoning: This channel is asset-side and liability-free, so it is orthogonal to the leverage, cash-runway and trade-credit measures already tested and is not the current-ratio filter listed as a single-theme anchor. Pairing it with the EBITDA multiple keeps the valuation leg insensitive to capital structure, so the interaction is cleanly "cheap operating earnings behind illiquid assets."
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap Post-Distress Turnaround
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(pi, at), 0), IND_RANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheap firms that have just returned to pretax profitability after a multi-year loss run are still priced on their distressed history; investors extrapolate the loss record, so the resolution of distress is under-reacted to and produces positive abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: The failed positive-polarity attempts all defined the healthy leg by *static* strength, which FF5's RMW and CMA already price; here the long leg requires a documented loss history plus a current profit, a state variable no factor spans. Firms still losing money receive zero and fall to the bottom of the sort, which is economically the correct short leg rather than an arbitrary neutral block.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Melting Book Value Cheapness
evaluated.hypothesis: Measured book-to-market is only meaningful if the book is stable; when a firm has destroyed a large cumulative amount of pretax income over five years, the reported equity is a melting asset that will be written down, so the apparent discount is an artifact of a stale numerator rather than a mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the stacking of four correlated distress ranks with one new construct — the *depth* of cumulative value destruction scaled by the asset base — which is economically distinct from the archive's loss *frequency* count because it distinguishes a firm with five shallow losses from one that has burned a third of its balance sheet. The mechanism explicitly attacks the measurement validity of the valuation leg, so the interaction is between cheapness and the credibility of the book value producing it, not two independent risk scores averaged together.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Thin Revenue Coverage of Liabilities
evaluated.hypothesis: Claims must ultimately be serviced out of business volume, so a cheap firm whose annual revenue is small relative to its total liabilities has no operating scale with which to grow out of its obligations, and its discount reflects a structural inability to service claims rather than temporary pessimism.
evaluated.reasoning: Revenue-to-liabilities is a scale-coverage measure that remains informative for loss-making firms, unlike the earnings, cash-runway and leverage channels already tested, and it does not require the profitability sign to be meaningful; this abandons the gate-times-z-score structure the critic identified as a twin of the failed within-cheap attempt. Coverage should be near the archive maximum because there are no temporal windows and no cash-flow-statement inputs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation-Floor Cheapness
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm's cash net of *all* liabilities covers a large share of its market capitalization, the equity has a hard floor and its cheapness cannot be a distress discount; such firms are cheap for non-fundamental reasons (neglect, forced selling) and should earn positive abnormal returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the flagged "value premium within levered firms" framing entirely and replaces it with a non-parametric separation of cheapness that is definitionally distress-free, which is the one positive-polarity story the archive has not tested — all prior positive attempts defined health through profitability or leverage scores that RMW and CMA already span. Because the numerator subtracts total liabilities rather than only debt, the measure is a genuine claim-adjusted valuation floor rather than an enterprise multiple, and the market-equity denominator is strictly positive so no sign inversion can occur.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Deep Tail Loss
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility is best summarized by the worst outcome the firm has recently proved capable of producing: a cheap firm whose deepest five-year pretax loss consumed a large share of assets has demonstrated tail exposure that investors treat as a lottery payoff rather than a risk.
evaluated.reasoning: Frequency (Signal 1) and dispersion (the accepted volatility signal) both worked while cumulative magnitude (Melting Book) did not, so the tail *minimum* discriminates between "how often" and "how bad" as the operative moment. TS_MIN is a distance-from-extreme construct rather than a sum, so it is not a rescaling of the cumulative-loss measure that already failed.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvent Liquidation-Floor Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(MA(RATIO(pi, at), 3), 0), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A claim-adjusted cash cushion is a genuine valuation floor only for firms that are actually earning money; among sustainably profitable firms, those whose market value is small relative to cash net of all liabilities are cheap without distress, while cash-burning shells with the same cushion are simply pre-liquidation.
evaluated.reasoning: The unconditional liquidation-floor measure produced a +3.9% FF5 alpha with a negative Sharpe and a wrong-signed FMB slope, the classic signature of a long leg of unprofitable cash shells with extreme negative RMW and CMA loadings; gating on a three-year average of positive pretax return on assets removes exactly those firms. Because the cushion enters as a centered z-score, unprofitable firms sit neutrally at zero and both extreme legs are profitable firms differing only in claim-adjusted cheapness.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapening Without Distress News
evaluated.hypothesis: A stock that has become much cheaper over the past year is a bargain only if the balance sheet did not deteriorate alongside the price; when liabilities rose over the same year, the discount is the market correctly capitalizing bad news, so identical price declines carry opposite information depending on the concurrent liability change.
evaluated.reasoning: This makes the interaction fully multiplicative in changes — magnitude from the size of the cheapening, sign from whether solvency improved or worsened — so firms with stable prices sit near zero and the spread is driven by the divergence between price news and fundamental news rather than by cheapness levels FF5 already prices. It is a distinct mechanism from the accepted distance-from-peak-leverage signal because it conditions on contemporaneous news flow rather than on a multi-year recovery state.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Unstable Capital Structure
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility can originate on the financing side rather than the operating side: a firm whose liability-to-asset ratio swings widely across years has no stable funding policy, is repeatedly forced into opportunistic borrowing or emergency repayment, and its cheapness therefore reflects genuine refinancing risk rather than a harvestable discount.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not an ablation of the chronic-loss trap because it contains no profitability input at all — it is the second moment of the *capital structure*, whereas the archive has only ever tested leverage levels, one-year changes, and distance from peak. Paired with the accepted profitability-volatility signal it answers a sharp question: is the fragility that FF5 cannot price an earnings phenomenon or a financing-policy phenomenon?
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Accelerating Working-Capital Drain
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquidity crises are convex: what predicts failure is not the level of working capital but the fact that its decline is speeding up, because an accelerating drain means the operating cycle is consuming cash faster each year and external financing must be obtained precisely when the equity is already depressed.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's liquidity evidence is entirely level-based (cash-to-current-liabilities), and its one change-based attempt mixed offsetting accrual effects; a second difference isolates deterioration in the *rate* of drain, which is a distinguishable state variable rather than a blend of tested proxies. If the trap alpha appears here without any loss or leverage input, the mechanism is imminent funding need rather than chronic unprofitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Tax-Validated Cheapness
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-tax expense is a costly, externally verified confirmation that reported profits are real; a cheap firm paying a normal effective tax rate has earnings the tax authority believes in, whereas a cheap firm with negligible or negative tax expense is either losing money or sheltering behind loss carryforwards accumulated in past distress.
evaluated.reasoning: The effective tax rate is close to scale-free and largely orthogonal to the profitability *level* that RMW prices, which is why it is a candidate for the positive polarity that static quality composites have failed to deliver; it also uses the tax channel, untested anywhere in the archive. Loss-making and NOL-sheltered firms fall naturally to the bottom of the second rank, so the short leg is cheap firms whose reported earnings carry no tax validation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity-Funded Burn Trap
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(GROWTH(csho, 1), NEG(RATIO(pi, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm that is losing money and simultaneously expanding its share count is financing its losses by selling equity at depressed prices, which transfers value from existing holders to new ones and makes the low multiple a measure of dilution ahead rather than value on offer.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested how distress is measured on the balance sheet and in the income statement but never how it is *financed*, and share-count growth is the observable footprint of distress funding for firms with no debt capacity left. The two severity inputs are complementary rather than redundant — issuance without losses is growth financing, losses without issuance means the firm is still self-funding — so the rank sum identifies the specific combination that destroys per-share value.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Eroding Claim Coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(sale, lt), 5), RATIO(sale, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Insolvency arrives when the business shrinks relative to its fixed claims; a cheap firm whose revenue-per-dollar-of-liabilities has fallen far below its own five-year peak is losing the operating scale that services those claims, and its multiple reflects a contracting franchise rather than a discount.
evaluated.reasoning: The level of revenue-to-liabilities produced only −1.4%/t=−1.56 because it is dominated by permanent industry differences in asset intensity, whereas distance from the firm's *own* peak isolates deterioration and is the mirror-image construct of the accepted distance-from-peak-leverage signal. It is also a scale channel rather than an earnings channel, so it remains informative for loss-making firms where the profitability moments are already saturated.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronically Cheap with Heavy Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness that has persisted for many consecutive years is qualitatively different from fresh cheapness: a firm that has sat in the cheap tail every year for half a decade while carrying a heavy claim load is structurally impaired rather than temporarily out of favour, and its discount will not converge.
evaluated.reasoning: Every valuation leg tested so far is a contemporaneous multiple, so the *duration* of cheapness is an entirely new dimension of the valuation theme rather than a noise-reduced average of multiples already tried. The interaction is economic, not cosmetic: persistent cheapness alone can reflect a stable low-growth business, and heavy liabilities alone are priced, but the combination identifies firms whose discount has been ratified by years of market judgment against a large fixed claim.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Worst-Case Burn Against Cash Buffer
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival is a ratio, not two scores: what matters is how much of the current cash balance a repeat of the firm's worst recent year would consume, so a cheap firm whose historical worst-case loss is large relative to its cash on hand is one bad year from recapitalisation.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than multiplying a tail-loss rank by a liquidity rank — which the critic rightly called a stack of two evaluated signals — this forms a single interpretable stress-test quantity, worst-case annual burn divided by the cash buffer, so the conditioning variation is the *ratio* and not the concentration of two extremes. The construct is scale-free, keeps the extreme portfolio broad because the ratio varies continuously across the whole cross-section, and is winsorised to control small-cash denominators.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Eroded-Book Wedge with Losses
evaluated.expression: MUL(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(pi, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm looks very cheap on sales but not on book, its book equity has already been consumed by write-downs and losses; combined with current unprofitability this wedge marks firms whose equity cushion is effectively gone, so the sales multiple overstates the shareholders' claim on the business.
evaluated.reasoning: The wedge between two multiples is a measure of accumulated equity erosion that no archive signal uses — all prior signals pick one multiple and treat the other as interchangeable — and it turns the inconsistency *between* valuation metrics into the distress diagnostic. Multiplying the signed wedge by loss intensity means the extreme legs are firms where a large wedge is accompanied by current losses, which is the specific state in which the cheap sales multiple is an illusion rather than a discount.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Long-Dated Liability Cheapness
evaluated.hypothesis: Holding the size of the claim load fixed, *when* it falls due determines whether a cheap firm can work through its problems; firms whose liabilities are predominantly long-dated have breathing room, so their discount is not a distress discount and should revert.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the net-net floor logic entirely and replaces it with liability maturity structure, a dimension of the distress theme the archive has never tested — every prior distress leg measured the amount, the trajectory, or the volatility of claims, never their timing. It also avoids the failure mode of previous positive-polarity attempts because a low current-liability share is not a profitability or asset-growth characteristic, so RMW and CMA have little reason to span it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Years Spent in the Trap Corner
evaluated.hypothesis: What identifies a value trap is not being cheap and levered today but having been cheap and levered year after year: repeated joint occupancy of the corner means the market has persistently refused to re-rate a firm whose claim load never lightens, so the discount is a permanent feature rather than a convergence opportunity.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best two signals both suggest persistence matters, but neither measures the persistence of the *interaction itself* — Chronic-Loss uses a contemporaneous multiple with a five-year loss count, and Chronically-Cheap uses cheapness duration with a contemporaneous liability level. Counting years in which both conditions hold simultaneously is a distinct construct that cannot be reproduced by multiplying two marginal ranks, and it needs no rank product at all, which keeps the extreme portfolios broad and stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Hidden Long-Dated Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-term liabilities that are neither current nor funded debt — pension shortfalls, deferred taxes, environmental and other accrued obligations — are opaque, non-negotiable claims that book equity flatters; a cheap firm carrying many of them is not cheap once these claims are recognised.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's one prior liability-composition test lumped all non-debt claims together and was dominated by current payables (alpha −1.6%, t=−1.29); isolating the *long-dated* non-debt residual targets exactly the claims that cannot be renegotiated in a restructuring and that no covenant discipline reveals early. Because these obligations sit outside both the current-ratio and leverage measures, the channel is orthogonal to everything tested so far.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Contributed-Not-Earned Equity
evaluated.hypothesis: The composition of book equity reveals whether a business has ever proven itself: a firm whose equity consists overwhelmingly of contributed capital rather than retained earnings has funded itself from investors instead of from operations, so its low multiple prices a business model that has never generated internal capital.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the flagged duration-plus-severity blend with an untested channel — the *earned share of equity*, a lifecycle-composition measure rather than a leverage, liquidity or profitability-moment proxy — so it cannot double-count the solvency inputs the critic identified. Unlike an accumulated-deficit level scaled by assets, the ratio to book equity is a composition statement, distinguishing a mature firm with modest retained earnings from a serially recapitalised one whose entire book is paid-in capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Thin Flow Coverage of Near-Term Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, txt), lct))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Near-term obligations are met out of annual operating cash generation net of cash taxes, so a cheap firm whose after-tax operating profit is small relative to its current liabilities must refinance every year regardless of how much cash it happens to hold today.
evaluated.reasoning: The revised distress leg is a *flow* coverage ratio of near-term claims and is monotone in the right direction throughout its range — negative EBITDA maps to the most severe end rather than flipping sign, which was the internal inconsistency in the EBITDA-minus-pretax-income construction. It complements the archive's stock-based cash-runway signal (che/lct, alpha −2.6%) by asking whether the firm can *earn* its way through the next year rather than whether it has already banked the cash.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap Dividend Cutters with Heavy Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(dvc, 1)), 0), RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Managers cut dividends only under genuine duress because the action is costly and public; a cheap firm that has just reduced its distribution while carrying a heavy claim load is revealing privately known distress, and the market underreacts to that admission.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the accruals-adjacent operating-asset channel and substitutes a payout *event*, which no archive signal uses — the one prior dividend test measured the level of payout coverage, not the act of cutting. The indicator switches the severity term on only for actual cutters and scales it by the claim load, so the high leg is cheap, levered firms with a fresh credible distress signal, while non-cutters (including the many firms with no dividend) contribute nothing to the severity rank.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Escaped the Trap Corner
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.6)), 5)), INDICATOR(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(lt, at), 5), RATIO(lt, at)), 0.15))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that spent years cheap and heavily levered but have now materially reduced their claim load relative to their own peak have resolved the condition that justified the discount, yet remain priced on their trap history, so the re-rating is still ahead of them.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the outlier-prone signed delta-leverage construction with a *state-transition* design: long-standing corner residency establishes the anchoring, and a discrete, economically meaningful exit condition (leverage at least fifteen points below its five-year peak) establishes resolution, so extreme portfolio membership is determined by persistent states rather than by one noisy annual change. It is the one positive-polarity form with a credible chance against FF5 because the long leg consists of formerly distressed levered firms, which carry weak RMW and CMA loadings, rather than the quality-value profile the factors have absorbed in every prior attempt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Centered Fragility Among Cheap Firms
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically interesting comparison is between cheap fragile and cheap robust firms; with severity centered rather than ranked, magnitude comes from cheapness and sign from fragility, so the short leg is cheap-and-fragile and the long leg is cheap-and-robust rather than expensive-and-robust.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one design choice — centering the severity leg — to fix the diagnosed reason our trap spreads have near-zero Sharpe despite reliable negative alpha: the low leg is currently a glamour basket whose raw return offsets the trap gain, and both legs should instead sit in the cheap tail so HML exposure largely cancels. Unlike the earlier within-cheap attempts, there is no indicator gate, so no zero block contaminates the extreme deciles and coverage is unchanged.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Secular Profit Decline
evaluated.hypothesis: A cheap firm whose pretax return on assets has been sliding steadily for five years is in secular decline rather than cyclical trough, and the market misreads the low multiple as a cyclical entry point when the earnings base is structurally eroding.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested the level, one-year change, volatility, worst realisation and cumulative sum of profitability, but never its *slope*, which distinguishes a firm at a stable low level from one on a monotone glide path — economically distinct states with the same average profitability. The trend is estimated over five years, so it is far less outlier-sensitive than the one-year delta that produced only −1.5%.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Financial Near-Term Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: Payables roll over automatically with the business, but maturing bank and market debt must be actively refinanced by a lender who can refuse; a cheap firm whose current liabilities are predominantly financial debt is one credit decision away from restructuring, while an identical firm financed by trade credit is not.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the near-term mirror of the archive's best new channel — Hidden Long-Dated Claims showed liability *composition* carries information where liability levels do not — and it isolates who holds the near-term claim rather than how large it is. It is also a cleaner test of refinancing risk than the cash-runway signal, which conflates the size of near-term claims with the firm's cash policy.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap with Maturity Mismatch
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(lct, SUB(at, act)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is triggered by funding long-lived, illiquid assets with claims that fall due within a year; a cheap firm with large current liabilities relative to its non-current asset base must either roll them or sell illiquid assets at fire-sale prices, and neither outcome leaves value for shareholders.
evaluated.reasoning: This is an asset-liability *matching* concept rather than a liquidity level or a leverage ratio: it compares the timing of claims with the liquidity of what they finance, which neither the current-ratio family nor the archive's act/at recovery-value test captures. The denominator, non-current assets, is positive for essentially all operating firms so the ratio is well behaved, and winsorising controls the asset-light tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap and Never Repaired
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(RATIO(lt, at), TS_MIN(RATIO(lt, at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Judge a firm's claim load against its own demonstrated capacity to operate with less: a cheap firm whose liabilities now sit far above the lightest balance sheet it has run in five years has taken on obligations it has shown no ability to shed, so the discount reflects an unresolved and self-inflicted solvency constraint rather than a cyclical low.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the smoothed cheap-times-leverage product with a firm-normalised construct — distance *above* the firm's own five-year leverage trough — which is the untested mirror of the archived distance-below-peak measure and, unlike a leverage level, is immune to permanent industry and business-model differences in normal indebtedness. It therefore tests whether the trap is about the absolute size of claims (already shown to be weak: level-based leverage signals produced alphas from −1.6% to +1.0%) or about a firm having drifted away from its own proven operating capital structure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Worst-Route Severity Among Cheap Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MAX(IND_RANK(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity is destroyed by whichever route is worst, not by the average of routes: a cheap firm with either a deep operating loss history or a large block of opaque long-dated claims is a trap, and being clean on the other dimension provides no offset.
evaluated.reasoning: Using MAX implements the union logic the hypothesis actually states, whereas SUMRANK was compensatory and pushed single-route firms to mid-scale — the internal inconsistency the critic identified — so this is a genuinely different aggregation function rather than a blend of two archived signals. Non-compensatory aggregation should also raise the alpha t-statistic because the high leg now contains every firm exposed on either route instead of only the rarer firms extreme on both.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Distressed Growth Versus Quality Growth
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, net indebtedness separates two very different businesses: a cash-rich franchise whose multiple is justified by durability, and a levered story stock whose multiple is a bet on refinancing; the second should badly underperform the first.
evaluated.reasoning: Centering the severity leg places both extreme portfolios in the expensive tail so the spread is HML-neutral by construction, which is exactly the transformation that produced the archive's cleanest sign reversal when applied in the cheap tail. Net debt scaled by assets is the channel with the widest coverage and no history of sign ambiguity, and pairing it with expensiveness rather than cheapness is the untested half of the interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Compensated Distress Inside Value
evaluated.hypothesis: Inside the cheap tail, distress is a priced risk rather than a mispricing: cheap levered firms earn returns that exceed what their factor loadings imply, while cheap unlevered firms are the group the value and profitability factors most over-reward.
evaluated.reasoning: This tests whether the gen-6 sign reversal is specific to earnings fragility or a general property of the cheap tail, using the liability-level channel that failed as a trap indicator but has never been tested in centered form. A confirmation with an independent distress dimension would settle the interpretation before the final two generations, and a failure would localise the compensated-distress result to the income statement.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Pure Valuation-Distress Interaction
evaluated.hypothesis: Stripping both main effects, the interaction itself should be positive: fragility is rewarded where the price is already low and punished where the price is high, so cheap-fragile and expensive-robust firms outperform cheap-robust and expensive-fragile ones.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal to date multiplies at least one uncentered rank and therefore carries a valuation or distress main effect that dominates the FMB slope; double centering isolates the cross-term, which is the object this research theme actually asks about. Its result is diagnostic regardless of sign: a reliable positive alpha would confirm that the whole archive has been measuring main effects contaminated by an interaction of the opposite sign.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Value Premium Inside the Fragile Group
evaluated.hypothesis: Holding fragility fixed, price does the discriminating: among firms with demonstrated deep-loss capacity, the cheaply priced ones are compensated for bearing that risk while the richly priced ones are lottery tickets, so the spread between cheap-fragile and dear-fragile firms should be positive.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the mirror decomposition of the accepted "Compensated Distress Inside Value" — that signal fixes cheapness and varies distress, this one fixes fragility and varies price — so the pair localises which dimension carries the interaction, and neither is a rank complement of an archived expression because the signed z-score makes the signal non-monotone in both themes. Magnitude is set by fragility and sign by valuation, so both extreme legs sit in the fragile tail and the spread is distress-neutral by construction rather than a restatement of expensive-junk underperformance.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear and Dependent on Short-Term Debt
evaluated.hypothesis: A rich multiple is only safe if the firm controls its own funding: among richly valued firms, those whose claim structure is concentrated in maturing financial debt depend on a lender's annual consent, while those funded long or by trade credit do not, so the first group's valuation is a refinancing bet.
evaluated.reasoning: The channel is the composition and maturity of financial claims — which delivered −1.9% (t=−1.96) in the cheap tail and is unrelated to issuance, profitability or asset growth, so no canonical anomaly or FF5 factor spans it. Centering places both legs inside the expensive tail, making the spread a clean quality-of-funding comparison among story stocks rather than the rank complement of anything already evaluated.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear with Unstable Fundamentals
evaluated.hypothesis: High multiples are justified by durable earning power; when a richly valued firm's pretax profitability instead swings widely from year to year, investors are paying a franchise price for a lottery distribution, and the stable franchises in the same valuation tier should outperform them.
evaluated.reasoning: Profitability volatility is a second moment, so unlike liability or asset growth it cannot be absorbed by the CMA investment factor or by the RMW level of profitability — which is exactly the objection that sank the debt-financed-expansion version. Centering the volatility leg keeps both portfolios among expensive firms, so the test isolates whether the market pays the same multiple for stable and unstable earnings streams, a comparison the archive has only ever run inside the cheap tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear with Hidden Long-Dated Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Opaque non-current, non-debt obligations — pension shortfalls, deferred taxes, accrued environmental and contractual claims — are the claims investors most easily overlook when paying a premium multiple, so richly valued firms carrying them should disappoint.
evaluated.reasoning: The hidden-claims channel produced −2.9% (t=−2.68) in the cheap tail, and testing it in the expensive tail establishes whether the newly discovered expensive-corner effect is specific to funded net debt or general to any senior claim, which is the key generalisation question before the final generation. Because these obligations are invisible to the leverage and current-ratio measures FF5 characteristics proxy for, the channel should not be absorbed by the investment or profitability factors.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear Without Taxable Income
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash taxes are the externally audited evidence that a business earns real money; among firms commanding rich revenue multiples, those paying little or no tax are being valued on a promise the tax authority sees no sign of, while their tax-paying peers at the same multiple have validated earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: Centering the tax leg keeps both extreme portfolios inside the expensive tail, so the comparison is between validated and unvalidated premium valuations rather than a repeat of the value-versus-growth sort. The tax channel is the one distress dimension in the resource menu that has been used only once, and it is conceptually distinct from leverage, liquidity and earnings moments because it measures verification rather than magnitude of profit.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Which Risk Is Paid For Inside Value
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at)), IND_RANK(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Inside the cheap tail the market prices earnings risk but not balance-sheet risk: value investors are compensated for volatile profitability, yet the same discount does not compensate for creditor claims, so cheap firms whose risk is financial rather than operating should underperform those whose risk is operating rather than financial.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly formalises the contradiction between the two centered cheap-tail results — earnings fragility earned +2.4% while leverage earned −2.9% — by sorting on the *wedge* between a firm's financial and operating risk rank rather than on either risk alone. Both legs are cheap firms with similar total risk, so the spread is nearly value-neutral and tests a specific claim about which risk dimension the value discount actually compensates.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear with Weak Claim Coverage
evaluated.hypothesis: A premium multiple is only defensible if the business generates enough operating profit to service the claims standing ahead of equity; among richly valued firms, those whose EBITDA is small relative to total liabilities are paying creditors out of future promises, while their well-covered peers at the same multiple are genuine franchises.
evaluated.reasoning: This retains the centered structure that produced the archive's largest alpha but changes the economic content of the severity leg from the *stock* of net debt to the *flow* coverage of all claims, so it is not a one-operator respecification and it does not reintroduce a monotone expensiveness main effect — both extreme portfolios remain inside the expensive tail. It also tests corner dependence directly: the same coverage channel was nearly worthless in the cheap tail (−0.6%, t=−0.57), so a large alpha here would establish that claim coverage matters only where the market has already paid a premium.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear with Either Risk Realised
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), MAX(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A premium valuation can be destroyed by either route — creditors holding a large net claim or a demonstrated capacity for deep operating losses — and being clean on one route provides no offset, so the worst of the two standardised risks is what should price the equity.
evaluated.reasoning: MAX over two z-scored risks implements the union logic the hypothesis actually states, replacing the rank-average that merely blended two documented main effects, and because both risk inputs are centered the low leg consists of expensive firms exposed to neither risk rather than of cheap firms. The two routes are economically distinct — one balance-sheet stock, one income-statement tail — so the union should broaden the short leg from the rare firms extreme on both to every premium-valued firm exposed on either, which is the route to a more reliable alpha t-statistic.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Long-Standing Premium With Net Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: A multiple that the market has sustained for years is a capitalised narrative rather than a transient re-rating; when such a firm also carries net debt, the story has been financed by creditors and any disappointment falls on equity first, so persistent premium plus net claims should underperform persistent premium with net cash.
evaluated.reasoning: This imports the duration mechanism that produced −3.2% (t=−2.49) in the cheap tail into the expensive corner where the archive's alpha now lives, so it is a new construct rather than a denominator swap, and it avoids the mechanical anti-correlation problem because the valuation leg is a count of years spent in the expensive tail rather than a leverage-contaminated level like ME/at. The count is ranked and then multiplied by a continuous centered severity, so the signal stays continuous and does not repeat the degenerate integer-portfolio failure of the gen-5 occupancy signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained Premium with Either Risk
evaluated.expression: MUL(MA(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), 5), MAX(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A multiple the market has sustained for five years is a capitalised narrative rather than a transient re-rating, and when such a firm is exposed to either creditor claims or deep-loss capacity the eventual disappointment is larger than for a firm whose premium is new.
evaluated.reasoning: The persistence idea produced the archive's largest alpha (−4.8%, t=−4.74) but a dead slope because the valuation leg was an integer occupancy count; replacing it with a five-year moving average of the expensiveness rank keeps the same economics as a smooth, monotone quantity. Pairing it with the union severity that fixed the slope in gen 8 is the single most promising combination the run has identified, and it is a construction repair rather than a new mechanism by design.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dear with Negative Working Capital
evaluated.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, those running negative working capital relative to their current obligations are funding the growth story with supplier and short-term credit, so any slowdown in the narrative immediately becomes a funding event rather than a valuation adjustment.
evaluated.reasoning: Working capital adequacy is the one balance-sheet channel never tested in the expensive tail, and it is distinct from the net-debt stock because it measures the operating cycle's self-funding rather than financial leverage. Centering keeps both legs inside the expensive tail, so the comparison is between self-funding and credit-dependent premium valuations rather than a repeat of a value sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained Premium with Rising Encumbrance
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What condemns a premium valuation is not the static level of creditor claims but the fact that the firm has drifted far above the lightest net-claim position it has proved it can operate with, because the narrative investors are paying for is now being financed by lenders rather than by the business.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a third collinear MAX arm with a genuinely different construct — distance above the firm's own five-year net-debt trough — which is firm-normalised and therefore immune to the permanent industry differences in indebtedness that a level ratio carries; the same own-history transformation produced the highest FMB slope in the cheap tail (4.00). Because the severity leg is centered, both extreme portfolios stay inside the expensive tail and the signal cannot collapse toward the sales-to-price main effect the critic warned about.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Revenue Premium with Eroding Margin
evaluated.hypothesis: A high price paid per dollar of revenue is a bet on future margins; when the pretax margin actually earned on that revenue has been sliding for five years, the multiple is being applied to a shrinking conversion rate and must contract.
evaluated.reasoning: This removes the internal inconsistency the critic identified — the severity leg is now a pure operating-margin trajectory with no liability scaling anywhere in the expression, so the flow interpretation is exact — and it pairs the valuation denominator (sales) with the precise fundamental (margin on sales) that justifies it, which no prior signal in the archive does. The margin path is a five-year slope rather than a level, so it is distinguishable from the profitability level RMW prices and from the ROA trend already tested in the cheap tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Premium Over Normalised Revenue with Net Claims
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), MA(sale, 3))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Expensiveness should be measured against normal, not momentary, revenue: a firm whose price is high relative to three-year average sales is genuinely richly valued, whereas a firm that looks expensive only because last year's revenue collapsed is a distressed firm mislabelled as a premium one.
evaluated.reasoning: This addresses a real construction hazard in the archive's best signals rather than swapping yardsticks for novelty: single-year sales in the denominator makes revenue collapse — itself a distress symptom correlated with the severity leg — masquerade as a high multiple, so smoothing separates the premium-valuation mechanism from the revenue-collapse mechanism. Unlike market-to-book it introduces no sign hazard, since three-year average sales is positive for essentially every firm, and coverage should remain near the archive maximum.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap and Deleveraging
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(TREND(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness plus a multi-year decline in the debt-to-assets state identifies firms whose distress risk is receding while the price still embeds the old distress discount, generating a repricing drift.
considered.reasoning: The level of leverage is slow-moving and largely priced, but the direction of the balance-sheet repair trend is under-reacted to, so pairing sales-to-price with a five-year deleveraging trend captures a dynamic interaction rather than two static levels. Cheap firms with rising leverage load the short leg, matching the trap narrative.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unjustified-Discount Gap
considered.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(MA(RATIO(ib, at), 3)))))
considered.hypothesis: Within an industry, the part of a firm's cheapness that is not matched by its distress ranking is mispricing; the part that is matched is fair compensation for default risk.
considered.reasoning: Differencing the industry rank of book-to-market against the industry rank of a fundamental distress score (leverage plus smoothed three-year profitability) yields an explicit residual-discount measure, so the signal is large only when a firm is cheap without a distress justification. Industry ranking removes sector-level leverage norms and multiple levels that would otherwise drive the spread.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Weakest-Link Cheap and Debt-Serviceable
considered.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dlc), lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The value premium is conjunctive rather than additive: a firm must be both cheap and able to cover its liabilities out of internally generated cash after current maturities, and failing either condition destroys the premium entirely rather than partially offsetting it.
considered.reasoning: MIN replaces the fixed-weight rank blend with a non-substitutable (Leontief) interaction, so a very high book-to-market can no longer compensate for weak debt-service capacity the way it does in a Piotroski-style additive score. The distress channel is a flow-versus-stock coverage measure, (oancf - dlc)/lt, rather than a leverage level, and firms with negative book equity or negative post-maturity cash flow are correctly pinned to the short leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Within-Cheap Health Dispersion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(oancf, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: All of the economically interesting variation lies inside the cheap segment: among value stocks, those with accumulated retained earnings and cash-flow coverage of liabilities are compensated value, while those without are distress traps, and non-cheap firms carry no directional information at all.
considered.reasoning: The gate is now placed on the valuation dimension, not the distress dimension, so the ranked variable driving the sort is a continuous health z-score measured only where the value story applies; the zero block is genuinely neutral (non-cheap firms) instead of dumping distressed names into the middle alongside healthy glamour firms. Both extreme legs are therefore populated exclusively by cheap firms sorted by solvency, which is a direct test of the healthy-versus-trap split rather than a restatement of a screened value strategy.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Refinancing-Burden-Net Cash Flow Yield
considered.hypothesis: Equity holders only own the operating cash flow that survives near-term debt repayment, so cash-flow yield should be charged for the current maturities the firm must roll; firms that look cheap on gross cash flow but face large short-term obligations are not cheap to equity.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the enterprise multiple, the denominator is market equity, which is strictly positive, so the cash-rich sign-inversion and negative-EV pathology cannot occur; the distress interaction enters the numerator as an explicit refinancing charge (dlc) against operating cash flow. This measures cheapness of the residual claim after rollover risk rather than cheapness of the whole capital structure, and it separates high-yield firms with distant maturities from high-yield firms whose cash is pre-committed to lenders.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap Intensity
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5), RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Lottery-like distress traps are firms whose price is low relative to sales precisely because they have repeatedly lost money and carry net debt they cannot retire; investors overpay for the small recovery option, so trap intensity predicts underperformance.
considered.reasoning: Cheapness is measured with sales-to-price, whose numerator and denominator are both positive, eliminating the negative-book-equity sign inversion that made the earlier version place the most distressed firms on the long leg. Distress severity is continuous and multi-year, blending the count of loss years over five years with net-debt-to-assets, so the sort has no degenerate mass of zeros and the product is maximal only for the cheap-and-chronically-impaired intersection.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash-Runway Value Trap
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, what predicts underperformance is not leverage per se but the absence of a near-term cash runway: cheap firms holding little cash against current liabilities must sell assets or issue equity at depressed prices, transferring value away from shareholders.
considered.reasoning: This deliberately strips out every solvency and profitability input so that the interaction rests on one clean liquidity channel, letting us attribute the trap alpha to funding capacity rather than to earnings quality already spanned by RMW. If it reproduces the trap alpha with no profitability ingredient, the mechanism is refinancing pressure; if it fails, the earlier alpha was a profitability effect in disguise.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Repaired-Balance-Sheet Cheapness
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(lt, at), 5), RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose leverage now sits far below its own five-year peak have completed a balance-sheet repair that removed the default risk originally responsible for the discount, but the discount persists because investors anchor on the prior distressed state.
considered.reasoning: Distance from a firm's own leverage maximum is a within-firm recovery measure that is not a cross-sectional quality score, so it should not be absorbed by RMW or CMA the way the failed healthy-cheapness composites were. This is the constructive counterpart to the trap signals: it asks whether the positive polarity can work at all once the healthy leg is defined by distress *resolution* rather than by static financial strength.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Own-History Distress Spiral
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 5))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is in a spiral when it is simultaneously at the cheapest point of its own valuation history and the most indebted point of its own balance-sheet history; this joint own-history extreme signals an ongoing deterioration that cross-sectional levels miss for firms that are permanently cheap or permanently levered.
considered.reasoning: Cross-sectional cheapness and leverage ranks are dominated by stable industry and business-model differences, whereas own-history positioning identifies firms actively moving into distress, which is a distinguishable economic mechanism rather than a rescaling of Signal 1. Because both legs contain firms at varying cross-sectional cheapness levels, the spread should carry small net HML exposure and hence be harder for FF5 to explain.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Trade-Credit-Squeezed Cheapness
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, ADD(dltt, dlc)), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms whose liability stack is dominated by non-debt claims (payables, accruals, pension and other operating obligations) rather than negotiated debt are squeezed by suppliers and counterparties who can withdraw credit without a restructuring process, so their apparent earnings cheapness accrues to those claimants rather than to shareholders.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the archive's net-debt/leverage channel entirely and replaces it with the composition of liabilities, a distinct distress mechanism: non-debt obligations carry no covenant renegotiation option, so operating creditors impose discipline exactly when the equity is already cheap. Pairing it with EBITDA-to-market rather than sales-to-market also changes the valuation leg to a margin-sensitive multiple, so the test is not a one-ingredient substitution into Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Twin Deterioration
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(pi, at), 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: For firms already trading at low multiples, the market underreacts to the joint direction of change in solvency and profitability: rising liabilities alongside falling pretax income confirms that the discount reflects genuine deterioration rather than temporary pessimism.
considered.reasoning: Both deterioration channels now move the same way with distress — a rise in liabilities-to-assets and a decline in pretax return on assets — removing the earlier accrual-anomaly sign conflict from the working-capital leg. Pretax income is used so the profitability trajectory is not contaminated by tax-benefit recognition, which is itself mechanically linked to distress.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payout-Coverage Mismatch Trap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(pi, txt), lct))))
considered.hypothesis: A high dividend yield is a value signal only when earnings comfortably cover near-term obligations; firms distributing cash while after-tax income is small relative to current liabilities are financing payout from a shrinking buffer, and the eventual dividend cut triggers a repricing and yield-investor exit.
considered.reasoning: This drops market leverage and market-scaled income entirely, so it no longer reproduces the Campbell-Hilscher-Szilagyi or Bhandari inputs; the distress leg is an accounting coverage ratio of after-tax earnings against current liabilities, and the valuation leg is the payout-based cheapness channel untested elsewhere in the archive. The interaction is genuinely conditional in economics: identical yields carry opposite information depending on whether the payout is covered, which is why the product form, not either leg alone, should predict returns.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Unstable Fundamentals
considered.hypothesis: The lottery half of the economic story is about the *variance* of fundamentals, not their level: a cheap firm whose pretax return on assets swings widely has an equity claim resembling an out-of-the-money option, and investors overpay for that skewness.
considered.reasoning: Every distress measure tested so far is a first-moment level or change; five-year volatility of pretax profitability is a second-moment channel that formalizes "lottery-like" without using leverage or losses at all. If this reproduces the trap alpha, the effect is about payoff convexity rather than solvency, which would substantially redirect the remaining search.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Low Recovery Value
considered.hypothesis: What makes cheapness dangerous is not the size of the claims but what shareholders would recover: a cheap firm whose assets are overwhelmingly illiquid and long-lived cannot raise cash without fire-sale discounts, so operating earnings never reach equity holders.
considered.reasoning: This channel is asset-side and liability-free, so it is orthogonal to the leverage, cash-runway and trade-credit measures already tested and is not the current-ratio filter listed as a single-theme anchor. Pairing it with the EBITDA multiple keeps the valuation leg insensitive to capital structure, so the interaction is cleanly "cheap operating earnings behind illiquid assets."
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Post-Distress Turnaround
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(pi, at), 0), IND_RANK(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Cheap firms that have just returned to pretax profitability after a multi-year loss run are still priced on their distressed history; investors extrapolate the loss record, so the resolution of distress is under-reacted to and produces positive abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: The failed positive-polarity attempts all defined the healthy leg by *static* strength, which FF5's RMW and CMA already price; here the long leg requires a documented loss history plus a current profit, a state variable no factor spans. Firms still losing money receive zero and fall to the bottom of the sort, which is economically the correct short leg rather than an arbitrary neutral block.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Melting Book Value Cheapness
considered.hypothesis: Measured book-to-market is only meaningful if the book is stable; when a firm has destroyed a large cumulative amount of pretax income over five years, the reported equity is a melting asset that will be written down, so the apparent discount is an artifact of a stale numerator rather than a mispricing.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the stacking of four correlated distress ranks with one new construct — the *depth* of cumulative value destruction scaled by the asset base — which is economically distinct from the archive's loss *frequency* count because it distinguishes a firm with five shallow losses from one that has burned a third of its balance sheet. The mechanism explicitly attacks the measurement validity of the valuation leg, so the interaction is between cheapness and the credibility of the book value producing it, not two independent risk scores averaged together.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Thin Revenue Coverage of Liabilities
considered.hypothesis: Claims must ultimately be serviced out of business volume, so a cheap firm whose annual revenue is small relative to its total liabilities has no operating scale with which to grow out of its obligations, and its discount reflects a structural inability to service claims rather than temporary pessimism.
considered.reasoning: Revenue-to-liabilities is a scale-coverage measure that remains informative for loss-making firms, unlike the earnings, cash-runway and leverage channels already tested, and it does not require the profitability sign to be meaningful; this abandons the gate-times-z-score structure the critic identified as a twin of the failed within-cheap attempt. Coverage should be near the archive maximum because there are no temporal windows and no cash-flow-statement inputs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Liquidation-Floor Cheapness
considered.hypothesis: When a firm's cash net of *all* liabilities covers a large share of its market capitalization, the equity has a hard floor and its cheapness cannot be a distress discount; such firms are cheap for non-fundamental reasons (neglect, forced selling) and should earn positive abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the flagged "value premium within levered firms" framing entirely and replaces it with a non-parametric separation of cheapness that is definitionally distress-free, which is the one positive-polarity story the archive has not tested — all prior positive attempts defined health through profitability or leverage scores that RMW and CMA already span. Because the numerator subtracts total liabilities rather than only debt, the measure is a genuine claim-adjusted valuation floor rather than an enterprise multiple, and the market-equity denominator is strictly positive so no sign inversion can occur.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Deep Tail Loss
considered.hypothesis: Fragility is best summarized by the worst outcome the firm has recently proved capable of producing: a cheap firm whose deepest five-year pretax loss consumed a large share of assets has demonstrated tail exposure that investors treat as a lottery payoff rather than a risk.
considered.reasoning: Frequency (Signal 1) and dispersion (the accepted volatility signal) both worked while cumulative magnitude (Melting Book) did not, so the tail *minimum* discriminates between "how often" and "how bad" as the operative moment. TS_MIN is a distance-from-extreme construct rather than a sum, so it is not a rescaling of the cumulative-loss measure that already failed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Solvent Liquidation-Floor Value
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(MA(RATIO(pi, at), 3), 0), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A claim-adjusted cash cushion is a genuine valuation floor only for firms that are actually earning money; among sustainably profitable firms, those whose market value is small relative to cash net of all liabilities are cheap without distress, while cash-burning shells with the same cushion are simply pre-liquidation.
considered.reasoning: The unconditional liquidation-floor measure produced a +3.9% FF5 alpha with a negative Sharpe and a wrong-signed FMB slope, the classic signature of a long leg of unprofitable cash shells with extreme negative RMW and CMA loadings; gating on a three-year average of positive pretax return on assets removes exactly those firms. Because the cushion enters as a centered z-score, unprofitable firms sit neutrally at zero and both extreme legs are profitable firms differing only in claim-adjusted cheapness.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheapening Without Distress News
considered.hypothesis: A stock that has become much cheaper over the past year is a bargain only if the balance sheet did not deteriorate alongside the price; when liabilities rose over the same year, the discount is the market correctly capitalizing bad news, so identical price declines carry opposite information depending on the concurrent liability change.
considered.reasoning: This makes the interaction fully multiplicative in changes — magnitude from the size of the cheapening, sign from whether solvency improved or worsened — so firms with stable prices sit near zero and the spread is driven by the divergence between price news and fundamental news rather than by cheapness levels FF5 already prices. It is a distinct mechanism from the accepted distance-from-peak-leverage signal because it conditions on contemporaneous news flow rather than on a multi-year recovery state.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Unstable Capital Structure
considered.hypothesis: Fragility can originate on the financing side rather than the operating side: a firm whose liability-to-asset ratio swings widely across years has no stable funding policy, is repeatedly forced into opportunistic borrowing or emergency repayment, and its cheapness therefore reflects genuine refinancing risk rather than a harvestable discount.
considered.reasoning: This is not an ablation of the chronic-loss trap because it contains no profitability input at all — it is the second moment of the *capital structure*, whereas the archive has only ever tested leverage levels, one-year changes, and distance from peak. Paired with the accepted profitability-volatility signal it answers a sharp question: is the fragility that FF5 cannot price an earnings phenomenon or a financing-policy phenomenon?
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Accelerating Working-Capital Drain
considered.hypothesis: Liquidity crises are convex: what predicts failure is not the level of working capital but the fact that its decline is speeding up, because an accelerating drain means the operating cycle is consuming cash faster each year and external financing must be obtained precisely when the equity is already depressed.
considered.reasoning: The archive's liquidity evidence is entirely level-based (cash-to-current-liabilities), and its one change-based attempt mixed offsetting accrual effects; a second difference isolates deterioration in the *rate* of drain, which is a distinguishable state variable rather than a blend of tested proxies. If the trap alpha appears here without any loss or leverage input, the mechanism is imminent funding need rather than chronic unprofitability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Tax-Validated Cheapness
considered.hypothesis: Cash-tax expense is a costly, externally verified confirmation that reported profits are real; a cheap firm paying a normal effective tax rate has earnings the tax authority believes in, whereas a cheap firm with negligible or negative tax expense is either losing money or sheltering behind loss carryforwards accumulated in past distress.
considered.reasoning: The effective tax rate is close to scale-free and largely orthogonal to the profitability *level* that RMW prices, which is why it is a candidate for the positive polarity that static quality composites have failed to deliver; it also uses the tax channel, untested anywhere in the archive. Loss-making and NOL-sheltered firms fall naturally to the bottom of the second rank, so the short leg is cheap firms whose reported earnings carry no tax validation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Equity-Funded Burn Trap
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(GROWTH(csho, 1), NEG(RATIO(pi, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: A cheap firm that is losing money and simultaneously expanding its share count is financing its losses by selling equity at depressed prices, which transfers value from existing holders to new ones and makes the low multiple a measure of dilution ahead rather than value on offer.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested how distress is measured on the balance sheet and in the income statement but never how it is *financed*, and share-count growth is the observable footprint of distress funding for firms with no debt capacity left. The two severity inputs are complementary rather than redundant — issuance without losses is growth financing, losses without issuance means the firm is still self-funding — so the rank sum identifies the specific combination that destroys per-share value.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Eroding Claim Coverage
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(sale, lt), 5), RATIO(sale, lt))))
considered.hypothesis: Insolvency arrives when the business shrinks relative to its fixed claims; a cheap firm whose revenue-per-dollar-of-liabilities has fallen far below its own five-year peak is losing the operating scale that services those claims, and its multiple reflects a contracting franchise rather than a discount.
considered.reasoning: The level of revenue-to-liabilities produced only −1.4%/t=−1.56 because it is dominated by permanent industry differences in asset intensity, whereas distance from the firm's *own* peak isolates deterioration and is the mirror-image construct of the accepted distance-from-peak-leverage signal. It is also a scale channel rather than an earnings channel, so it remains informative for loss-making firms where the profitability moments are already saturated.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Chronically Cheap with Heavy Claims
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness that has persisted for many consecutive years is qualitatively different from fresh cheapness: a firm that has sat in the cheap tail every year for half a decade while carrying a heavy claim load is structurally impaired rather than temporarily out of favour, and its discount will not converge.
considered.reasoning: Every valuation leg tested so far is a contemporaneous multiple, so the *duration* of cheapness is an entirely new dimension of the valuation theme rather than a noise-reduced average of multiples already tried. The interaction is economic, not cosmetic: persistent cheapness alone can reflect a stable low-growth business, and heavy liabilities alone are priced, but the combination identifies firms whose discount has been ratified by years of market judgment against a large fixed claim.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Worst-Case Burn Against Cash Buffer
