considered.hypothesis: Survival is a ratio, not two scores: what matters is how much of the current cash balance a repeat of the firm's worst recent year would consume, so a cheap firm whose historical worst-case loss is large relative to its cash on hand is one bad year from recapitalisation.
considered.reasoning: Rather than multiplying a tail-loss rank by a liquidity rank — which the critic rightly called a stack of two evaluated signals — this forms a single interpretable stress-test quantity, worst-case annual burn divided by the cash buffer, so the conditioning variation is the *ratio* and not the concentration of two extremes. The construct is scale-free, keeps the extreme portfolio broad because the ratio varies continuously across the whole cross-section, and is winsorised to control small-cash denominators.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Eroded-Book Wedge with Losses
considered.expression: MUL(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(pi, at))))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm looks very cheap on sales but not on book, its book equity has already been consumed by write-downs and losses; combined with current unprofitability this wedge marks firms whose equity cushion is effectively gone, so the sales multiple overstates the shareholders' claim on the business.
considered.reasoning: The wedge between two multiples is a measure of accumulated equity erosion that no archive signal uses — all prior signals pick one multiple and treat the other as interchangeable — and it turns the inconsistency *between* valuation metrics into the distress diagnostic. Multiplying the signed wedge by loss intensity means the extreme legs are firms where a large wedge is accompanied by current losses, which is the specific state in which the cheap sales multiple is an illusion rather than a discount.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Long-Dated Liability Cheapness
considered.hypothesis: Holding the size of the claim load fixed, *when* it falls due determines whether a cheap firm can work through its problems; firms whose liabilities are predominantly long-dated have breathing room, so their discount is not a distress discount and should revert.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the net-net floor logic entirely and replaces it with liability maturity structure, a dimension of the distress theme the archive has never tested — every prior distress leg measured the amount, the trajectory, or the volatility of claims, never their timing. It also avoids the failure mode of previous positive-polarity attempts because a low current-liability share is not a profitability or asset-growth characteristic, so RMW and CMA have little reason to span it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Years Spent in the Trap Corner
considered.hypothesis: What identifies a value trap is not being cheap and levered today but having been cheap and levered year after year: repeated joint occupancy of the corner means the market has persistently refused to re-rate a firm whose claim load never lightens, so the discount is a permanent feature rather than a convergence opportunity.
considered.reasoning: The archive's best two signals both suggest persistence matters, but neither measures the persistence of the *interaction itself* — Chronic-Loss uses a contemporaneous multiple with a five-year loss count, and Chronically-Cheap uses cheapness duration with a contemporaneous liability level. Counting years in which both conditions hold simultaneously is a distinct construct that cannot be reproduced by multiplying two marginal ranks, and it needs no rank product at all, which keeps the extreme portfolios broad and stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Hidden Long-Dated Claims
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Long-term liabilities that are neither current nor funded debt — pension shortfalls, deferred taxes, environmental and other accrued obligations — are opaque, non-negotiable claims that book equity flatters; a cheap firm carrying many of them is not cheap once these claims are recognised.
considered.reasoning: The archive's one prior liability-composition test lumped all non-debt claims together and was dominated by current payables (alpha −1.6%, t=−1.29); isolating the *long-dated* non-debt residual targets exactly the claims that cannot be renegotiated in a restructuring and that no covenant discipline reveals early. Because these obligations sit outside both the current-ratio and leverage measures, the channel is orthogonal to everything tested so far.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Contributed-Not-Earned Equity
considered.hypothesis: The composition of book equity reveals whether a business has ever proven itself: a firm whose equity consists overwhelmingly of contributed capital rather than retained earnings has funded itself from investors instead of from operations, so its low multiple prices a business model that has never generated internal capital.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the flagged duration-plus-severity blend with an untested channel — the *earned share of equity*, a lifecycle-composition measure rather than a leverage, liquidity or profitability-moment proxy — so it cannot double-count the solvency inputs the critic identified. Unlike an accumulated-deficit level scaled by assets, the ratio to book equity is a composition statement, distinguishing a mature firm with modest retained earnings from a serially recapitalised one whose entire book is paid-in capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Thin Flow Coverage of Near-Term Claims
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, txt), lct))))
considered.hypothesis: Near-term obligations are met out of annual operating cash generation net of cash taxes, so a cheap firm whose after-tax operating profit is small relative to its current liabilities must refinance every year regardless of how much cash it happens to hold today.
considered.reasoning: The revised distress leg is a *flow* coverage ratio of near-term claims and is monotone in the right direction throughout its range — negative EBITDA maps to the most severe end rather than flipping sign, which was the internal inconsistency in the EBITDA-minus-pretax-income construction. It complements the archive's stock-based cash-runway signal (che/lct, alpha −2.6%) by asking whether the firm can *earn* its way through the next year rather than whether it has already banked the cash.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Dividend Cutters with Heavy Claims
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MUL(INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(dvc, 1)), 0), RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Managers cut dividends only under genuine duress because the action is costly and public; a cheap firm that has just reduced its distribution while carrying a heavy claim load is revealing privately known distress, and the market underreacts to that admission.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the accruals-adjacent operating-asset channel and substitutes a payout *event*, which no archive signal uses — the one prior dividend test measured the level of payout coverage, not the act of cutting. The indicator switches the severity term on only for actual cutters and scales it by the claim load, so the high leg is cheap, levered firms with a fresh credible distress signal, while non-cutters (including the many firms with no dividend) contribute nothing to the severity rank.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Escaped the Trap Corner
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.7), INDICATOR(RATIO(lt, at), 0.6)), 5)), INDICATOR(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(lt, at), 5), RATIO(lt, at)), 0.15))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that spent years cheap and heavily levered but have now materially reduced their claim load relative to their own peak have resolved the condition that justified the discount, yet remain priced on their trap history, so the re-rating is still ahead of them.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the outlier-prone signed delta-leverage construction with a *state-transition* design: long-standing corner residency establishes the anchoring, and a discrete, economically meaningful exit condition (leverage at least fifteen points below its five-year peak) establishes resolution, so extreme portfolio membership is determined by persistent states rather than by one noisy annual change. It is the one positive-polarity form with a credible chance against FF5 because the long leg consists of formerly distressed levered firms, which carry weak RMW and CMA loadings, rather than the quality-value profile the factors have absorbed in every prior attempt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Centered Fragility Among Cheap Firms
considered.hypothesis: The economically interesting comparison is between cheap fragile and cheap robust firms; with severity centered rather than ranked, magnitude comes from cheapness and sign from fragility, so the short leg is cheap-and-fragile and the long leg is cheap-and-robust rather than expensive-and-robust.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one design choice — centering the severity leg — to fix the diagnosed reason our trap spreads have near-zero Sharpe despite reliable negative alpha: the low leg is currently a glamour basket whose raw return offsets the trap gain, and both legs should instead sit in the cheap tail so HML exposure largely cancels. Unlike the earlier within-cheap attempts, there is no indicator gate, so no zero block contaminates the extreme deciles and coverage is unchanged.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Secular Profit Decline
considered.hypothesis: A cheap firm whose pretax return on assets has been sliding steadily for five years is in secular decline rather than cyclical trough, and the market misreads the low multiple as a cyclical entry point when the earnings base is structurally eroding.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested the level, one-year change, volatility, worst realisation and cumulative sum of profitability, but never its *slope*, which distinguishes a firm at a stable low level from one on a monotone glide path — economically distinct states with the same average profitability. The trend is estimated over five years, so it is far less outlier-sensitive than the one-year delta that produced only −1.5%.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Financial Near-Term Claims
considered.hypothesis: Payables roll over automatically with the business, but maturing bank and market debt must be actively refinanced by a lender who can refuse; a cheap firm whose current liabilities are predominantly financial debt is one credit decision away from restructuring, while an identical firm financed by trade credit is not.
considered.reasoning: This is the near-term mirror of the archive's best new channel — Hidden Long-Dated Claims showed liability *composition* carries information where liability levels do not — and it isolates who holds the near-term claim rather than how large it is. It is also a cleaner test of refinancing risk than the cash-runway signal, which conflates the size of near-term claims with the firm's cash policy.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap with Maturity Mismatch
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(lct, SUB(at, act)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Distress is triggered by funding long-lived, illiquid assets with claims that fall due within a year; a cheap firm with large current liabilities relative to its non-current asset base must either roll them or sell illiquid assets at fire-sale prices, and neither outcome leaves value for shareholders.
considered.reasoning: This is an asset-liability *matching* concept rather than a liquidity level or a leverage ratio: it compares the timing of claims with the liquidity of what they finance, which neither the current-ratio family nor the archive's act/at recovery-value test captures. The denominator, non-current assets, is positive for essentially all operating firms so the ratio is well behaved, and winsorising controls the asset-light tail.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap and Never Repaired
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUB(RATIO(lt, at), TS_MIN(RATIO(lt, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: Judge a firm's claim load against its own demonstrated capacity to operate with less: a cheap firm whose liabilities now sit far above the lightest balance sheet it has run in five years has taken on obligations it has shown no ability to shed, so the discount reflects an unresolved and self-inflicted solvency constraint rather than a cyclical low.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the smoothed cheap-times-leverage product with a firm-normalised construct — distance *above* the firm's own five-year leverage trough — which is the untested mirror of the archived distance-below-peak measure and, unlike a leverage level, is immune to permanent industry and business-model differences in normal indebtedness. It therefore tests whether the trap is about the absolute size of claims (already shown to be weak: level-based leverage signals produced alphas from −1.6% to +1.0%) or about a firm having drifted away from its own proven operating capital structure.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Worst-Route Severity Among Cheap Firms
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MAX(IND_RANK(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Equity is destroyed by whichever route is worst, not by the average of routes: a cheap firm with either a deep operating loss history or a large block of opaque long-dated claims is a trap, and being clean on the other dimension provides no offset.
considered.reasoning: Using MAX implements the union logic the hypothesis actually states, whereas SUMRANK was compensatory and pushed single-route firms to mid-scale — the internal inconsistency the critic identified — so this is a genuinely different aggregation function rather than a blend of two archived signals. Non-compensatory aggregation should also raise the alpha t-statistic because the high leg now contains every firm exposed on either route instead of only the rarer firms extreme on both.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Distressed Growth Versus Quality Growth
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, net indebtedness separates two very different businesses: a cash-rich franchise whose multiple is justified by durability, and a levered story stock whose multiple is a bet on refinancing; the second should badly underperform the first.
considered.reasoning: Centering the severity leg places both extreme portfolios in the expensive tail so the spread is HML-neutral by construction, which is exactly the transformation that produced the archive's cleanest sign reversal when applied in the cheap tail. Net debt scaled by assets is the channel with the widest coverage and no history of sign ambiguity, and pairing it with expensiveness rather than cheapness is the untested half of the interaction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Compensated Distress Inside Value
considered.hypothesis: Inside the cheap tail, distress is a priced risk rather than a mispricing: cheap levered firms earn returns that exceed what their factor loadings imply, while cheap unlevered firms are the group the value and profitability factors most over-reward.
considered.reasoning: This tests whether the gen-6 sign reversal is specific to earnings fragility or a general property of the cheap tail, using the liability-level channel that failed as a trap indicator but has never been tested in centered form. A confirmation with an independent distress dimension would settle the interpretation before the final two generations, and a failure would localise the compensated-distress result to the income statement.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Pure Valuation-Distress Interaction
considered.hypothesis: Stripping both main effects, the interaction itself should be positive: fragility is rewarded where the price is already low and punished where the price is high, so cheap-fragile and expensive-robust firms outperform cheap-robust and expensive-fragile ones.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal to date multiplies at least one uncentered rank and therefore carries a valuation or distress main effect that dominates the FMB slope; double centering isolates the cross-term, which is the object this research theme actually asks about. Its result is diagnostic regardless of sign: a reliable positive alpha would confirm that the whole archive has been measuring main effects contaminated by an interaction of the opposite sign.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Value Premium Inside the Fragile Group
considered.hypothesis: Holding fragility fixed, price does the discriminating: among firms with demonstrated deep-loss capacity, the cheaply priced ones are compensated for bearing that risk while the richly priced ones are lottery tickets, so the spread between cheap-fragile and dear-fragile firms should be positive.
considered.reasoning: This is the mirror decomposition of the accepted "Compensated Distress Inside Value" — that signal fixes cheapness and varies distress, this one fixes fragility and varies price — so the pair localises which dimension carries the interaction, and neither is a rank complement of an archived expression because the signed z-score makes the signal non-monotone in both themes. Magnitude is set by fragility and sign by valuation, so both extreme legs sit in the fragile tail and the spread is distress-neutral by construction rather than a restatement of expensive-junk underperformance.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear and Dependent on Short-Term Debt
considered.hypothesis: A rich multiple is only safe if the firm controls its own funding: among richly valued firms, those whose claim structure is concentrated in maturing financial debt depend on a lender's annual consent, while those funded long or by trade credit do not, so the first group's valuation is a refinancing bet.
considered.reasoning: The channel is the composition and maturity of financial claims — which delivered −1.9% (t=−1.96) in the cheap tail and is unrelated to issuance, profitability or asset growth, so no canonical anomaly or FF5 factor spans it. Centering places both legs inside the expensive tail, making the spread a clean quality-of-funding comparison among story stocks rather than the rank complement of anything already evaluated.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Unstable Fundamentals
considered.hypothesis: High multiples are justified by durable earning power; when a richly valued firm's pretax profitability instead swings widely from year to year, investors are paying a franchise price for a lottery distribution, and the stable franchises in the same valuation tier should outperform them.
considered.reasoning: Profitability volatility is a second moment, so unlike liability or asset growth it cannot be absorbed by the CMA investment factor or by the RMW level of profitability — which is exactly the objection that sank the debt-financed-expansion version. Centering the volatility leg keeps both portfolios among expensive firms, so the test isolates whether the market pays the same multiple for stable and unstable earnings streams, a comparison the archive has only ever run inside the cheap tail.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Hidden Long-Dated Claims
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(lt, lct), dltt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Opaque non-current, non-debt obligations — pension shortfalls, deferred taxes, accrued environmental and contractual claims — are the claims investors most easily overlook when paying a premium multiple, so richly valued firms carrying them should disappoint.
considered.reasoning: The hidden-claims channel produced −2.9% (t=−2.68) in the cheap tail, and testing it in the expensive tail establishes whether the newly discovered expensive-corner effect is specific to funded net debt or general to any senior claim, which is the key generalisation question before the final generation. Because these obligations are invisible to the leverage and current-ratio measures FF5 characteristics proxy for, the channel should not be absorbed by the investment or profitability factors.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear Without Taxable Income
considered.hypothesis: Cash taxes are the externally audited evidence that a business earns real money; among firms commanding rich revenue multiples, those paying little or no tax are being valued on a promise the tax authority sees no sign of, while their tax-paying peers at the same multiple have validated earnings.
considered.reasoning: Centering the tax leg keeps both extreme portfolios inside the expensive tail, so the comparison is between validated and unvalidated premium valuations rather than a repeat of the value-versus-growth sort. The tax channel is the one distress dimension in the resource menu that has been used only once, and it is conceptually distinct from leverage, liquidity and earnings moments because it measures verification rather than magnitude of profit.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Which Risk Is Paid For Inside Value
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at)), IND_RANK(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))))
considered.hypothesis: Inside the cheap tail the market prices earnings risk but not balance-sheet risk: value investors are compensated for volatile profitability, yet the same discount does not compensate for creditor claims, so cheap firms whose risk is financial rather than operating should underperform those whose risk is operating rather than financial.
considered.reasoning: This directly formalises the contradiction between the two centered cheap-tail results — earnings fragility earned +2.4% while leverage earned −2.9% — by sorting on the *wedge* between a firm's financial and operating risk rank rather than on either risk alone. Both legs are cheap firms with similar total risk, so the spread is nearly value-neutral and tests a specific claim about which risk dimension the value discount actually compensates.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Weak Claim Coverage
considered.hypothesis: A premium multiple is only defensible if the business generates enough operating profit to service the claims standing ahead of equity; among richly valued firms, those whose EBITDA is small relative to total liabilities are paying creditors out of future promises, while their well-covered peers at the same multiple are genuine franchises.
considered.reasoning: This retains the centered structure that produced the archive's largest alpha but changes the economic content of the severity leg from the *stock* of net debt to the *flow* coverage of all claims, so it is not a one-operator respecification and it does not reintroduce a monotone expensiveness main effect — both extreme portfolios remain inside the expensive tail. It also tests corner dependence directly: the same coverage channel was nearly worthless in the cheap tail (−0.6%, t=−0.57), so a large alpha here would establish that claim coverage matters only where the market has already paid a premium.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Either Risk Realised
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), MAX(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A premium valuation can be destroyed by either route — creditors holding a large net claim or a demonstrated capacity for deep operating losses — and being clean on one route provides no offset, so the worst of the two standardised risks is what should price the equity.
considered.reasoning: MAX over two z-scored risks implements the union logic the hypothesis actually states, replacing the rank-average that merely blended two documented main effects, and because both risk inputs are centered the low leg consists of expensive firms exposed to neither risk rather than of cheap firms. The two routes are economically distinct — one balance-sheet stock, one income-statement tail — so the union should broaden the short leg from the rare firms extreme on both to every premium-valued firm exposed on either, which is the route to a more reliable alpha t-statistic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Long-Standing Premium With Net Claims
considered.hypothesis: A multiple that the market has sustained for years is a capitalised narrative rather than a transient re-rating; when such a firm also carries net debt, the story has been financed by creditors and any disappointment falls on equity first, so persistent premium plus net claims should underperform persistent premium with net cash.
considered.reasoning: This imports the duration mechanism that produced −3.2% (t=−2.49) in the cheap tail into the expensive corner where the archive's alpha now lives, so it is a new construct rather than a denominator swap, and it avoids the mechanical anti-correlation problem because the valuation leg is a count of years spent in the expensive tail rather than a leverage-contaminated level like ME/at. The count is ranked and then multiplied by a continuous centered severity, so the signal stays continuous and does not repeat the degenerate integer-portfolio failure of the gen-5 occupancy signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sustained Premium with Either Risk
considered.expression: MUL(MA(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), 5), MAX(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, at), 5)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A multiple the market has sustained for five years is a capitalised narrative rather than a transient re-rating, and when such a firm is exposed to either creditor claims or deep-loss capacity the eventual disappointment is larger than for a firm whose premium is new.
considered.reasoning: The persistence idea produced the archive's largest alpha (−4.8%, t=−4.74) but a dead slope because the valuation leg was an integer occupancy count; replacing it with a five-year moving average of the expensiveness rank keeps the same economics as a smooth, monotone quantity. Pairing it with the union severity that fixed the slope in gen 8 is the single most promising combination the run has identified, and it is a construction repair rather than a new mechanism by design.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Negative Working Capital
considered.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, those running negative working capital relative to their current obligations are funding the growth story with supplier and short-term credit, so any slowdown in the narrative immediately becomes a funding event rather than a valuation adjustment.
considered.reasoning: Working capital adequacy is the one balance-sheet channel never tested in the expensive tail, and it is distinct from the net-debt stock because it measures the operating cycle's self-funding rather than financial leverage. Centering keeps both legs inside the expensive tail, so the comparison is between self-funding and credit-dependent premium valuations rather than a repeat of a value sort.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sustained Premium with Rising Encumbrance
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), sale)), IND_ZSCORE(SUB(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: What condemns a premium valuation is not the static level of creditor claims but the fact that the firm has drifted far above the lightest net-claim position it has proved it can operate with, because the narrative investors are paying for is now being financed by lenders rather than by the business.
considered.reasoning: This replaces a third collinear MAX arm with a genuinely different construct — distance above the firm's own five-year net-debt trough — which is firm-normalised and therefore immune to the permanent industry differences in indebtedness that a level ratio carries; the same own-history transformation produced the highest FMB slope in the cheap tail (4.00). Because the severity leg is centered, both extreme portfolios stay inside the expensive tail and the signal cannot collapse toward the sales-to-price main effect the critic warned about.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Revenue Premium with Eroding Margin
considered.hypothesis: A high price paid per dollar of revenue is a bet on future margins; when the pretax margin actually earned on that revenue has been sliding for five years, the multiple is being applied to a shrinking conversion rate and must contract.
considered.reasoning: This removes the internal inconsistency the critic identified — the severity leg is now a pure operating-margin trajectory with no liability scaling anywhere in the expression, so the flow interpretation is exact — and it pairs the valuation denominator (sales) with the precise fundamental (margin on sales) that justifies it, which no prior signal in the archive does. The margin path is a five-year slope rather than a level, so it is distinguishable from the profitability level RMW prices and from the ROA trend already tested in the cheap tail.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Premium Over Normalised Revenue with Net Claims
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), MA(sale, 3))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Expensiveness should be measured against normal, not momentary, revenue: a firm whose price is high relative to three-year average sales is genuinely richly valued, whereas a firm that looks expensive only because last year's revenue collapsed is a distressed firm mislabelled as a premium one.
considered.reasoning: This addresses a real construction hazard in the archive's best signals rather than swapping yardsticks for novelty: single-year sales in the denominator makes revenue collapse — itself a distress symptom correlated with the severity leg — masquerade as a high multiple, so smoothing separates the premium-valuation mechanism from the revenue-collapse mechanism. Unlike market-to-book it introduces no sign hazard, since three-year average sales is positive for essentially every firm, and coverage should remain near the archive maximum.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Dear with Heavy Near-Term Maturities
considered.hypothesis: Among richly valued firms, the binding constraint is how much debt must be repaid or rolled in the coming year relative to the size of the business generating the cash; a large annual maturity burden means a lender, not the market, decides whether the growth story continues.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the pure aggregation-operator swap with a distinct economic quantity — near-term maturities scaled by business volume — which measures refinancing *intensity* rather than the claim-composition share (dlc/lt) already tested or the stock of net debt in the archive winner. Scaling by revenue keeps the ratio positive and well behaved for loss-making firms, and centering keeps both legs among premium-valued firms so the spread compares refinancing-dependent with self-determining growth stories.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: This is a straightforward value-plus-financial-health composite that reproduces the well-documented Piotroski (2000) / quality-value screen with no new economic content, and the nested SUMRANK simply forms a fixed-weight linear rank blend rather than a genuine interaction.

critic_notes.target_name: Gated Cheapness on Retained Earnings and Working Capital
critic_notes.rationale: The gate assigns exactly zero to distressed firms, which does not "switch off" the signal but instead dumps them into the middle of the cross-section alongside healthy low-BM firms, corrupting both legs; the raw unwinsorized BM level and the Altman-component gates also make this a mechanical restatement of the known distress-screened value strategy.

This is literally the enterprise multiple (EBITDA/EV), a canonical published anomaly (Loughran and Wellman 2011), and it additionally suffers the standard negative/near-zero enterprise-value denominator problem that inverts the signal for cash-rich firms.

The expression is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis because the most distressed firms often have negative book equity, giving them a negative BM and thus a positive-tail signal value that places them on the wrong leg, and the near-universal zeros for profitable firms make the portfolio sort degenerate rather than a clean short of lottery-like distress.

Pairing sales-to-price with a multi-year leverage-trajectory (as opposed to level) is a defensible dynamic interaction that is not a direct restatement of a single published anomaly, though it sits close to the net-debt-issuance literature and the five-year TREND requirement will meaningfully reduce coverage and tilt toward older, surviving firms.

Industry-neutralizing both the cheapness rank and a distress rank is the best-constructed proposal here and the "discount unexplained by distress" framing is coherent, but a difference of ranks is monotone-equivalent to an equal-weighted linear blend rather than a true residual, making it substantially redundant with Signal 1.

This is a one-ingredient substitution into the archive's already-tested Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap (same sale/market-cap leg, same net-debt leg, loss-count swapped for the retained-earnings deficit that a second archive signal already used), so it is a cosmetic variant rather than a new mechanism, and the RE-based leg additionally overlaps the published retained-earnings-to-market decomposition of the value premium.

Internally consistent and deliberately minimal — a single funding-liquidity channel interacted with book-to-market, with a genuine diagnostic purpose and high expected coverage — though it is a simple two-way product of two well-known variables and its incremental content over the cash-holdings/distress literature is modest.

The second deterioration leg is sign-inconsistent with the stated hypothesis: NEG(DELTA(wcap/lct)) rewards *falling* working capital, which is low accruals and therefore predicts higher returns under the accrual anomaly, directly opposing the expected negative sign carried by the leverage-increase leg, so the SUMRANK mixes two offsetting known effects.

Debt-to-market-equity combined with a market-scaled profitability/loss term is essentially a hand-rolled version of the Campbell-Hilscher-Szilagyi failure-probability inputs (TLMTA plus NIMTA) and Bhandari leverage, making it a direct rediscovery of the published distress anomaly rather than a cross-theme interaction.

The within-firm distance-from-peak-leverage leg is a genuinely different construct from the static quality scores that failed earlier and gives the positive polarity a coherent anchoring story, with the caveat that deleveraging driven by asset or equity growth will load on CMA and should be diagnosed if the alpha appears.

Replacing both cross-sectional ranks with own-history percentiles is a substantive structural change that plausibly escapes industry/business-model level effects, but the B/M time-series rank leg is largely a multi-year price-decline proxy, so the signal risks being a repackaging of long-horizon reversal interacted with the known momentum-in-distressed-firms result and needs a control for past return.

This is a mechanical re-stacking of components already tested in the archive (the chronic-loss/net-debt pair is literally the severity score from "Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap Intensity," plus the cash-runway and leverage-delta terms), so it is a cosmetic aggregation rather than a new economic channel, and averaging four correlated distress ranks will most likely just dilute the one leg (loss persistence) that actually carried the alpha.

Structurally this is the sign-flipped twin of the archive's failed "Within-Cheap Health Dispersion" (same INDICATOR gate × IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(...)) form, gate moved 0.7→0.6, health→severity with the already-tested (lt−che)/at inside), and the only substantive novelty is the wcap/lct term and the coverage fix, which is a parameter/input tweak rather than a distinct mechanism.

The expression cleanly matches the hypothesis and the sign is natural, and while earnings volatility as a standalone negative predictor is published (Dichev–Tang and the low-risk/lottery literature), the second-moment interaction with cheapness is genuinely orthogonal to every first-moment distress channel in the archive and would be diagnostically informative either way.

Internally consistent and a genuinely asset-side channel not yet tested here, but the expected negative sign runs against the published asset-liquidity/tangibility evidence (illiquid-asset firms earn *higher* expected returns, Ortiz-Molina–Phillips), and act/at is close to a crude current-ratio restatement, so the prior on success is modest.

The indicator semantics match the stated hypothesis (currently profitable × loss-streak length × cheap), the positive sign is the natural direction of the expression, and conditioning on *resolution* of distress rather than static quality is a real state-variable distinction from the archive's failed positive-polarity attempts — though the large zero block of loss-making firms will make the short leg a mixture and should be diagnosed if the alpha is weak.

critic_notes.target_name: Value Premium Inside the Levered Group
critic_notes.rationale: Stripped of framing this is just book-to-market within a high-leverage subsample with the sign inverted, which is both a trivial restriction of the most-published anomaly in finance and contradicted by the direct prior evidence that the value premium is *largest* among high-distress-risk firms (Griffin–Lemmon), so the expected sign is at odds with the expression's established natural direction.

This is the archive's "Chronic-Loss Net-Debt Trap Intensity" with one SUMRANK leg deleted and `ib` swapped for `pi` — a component ablation rather than a new mechanism, and the surviving content (value × chronic unprofitability) is the textbook distress/profitability-tilted value trap.

Internally consistent and the worst-realization moment is genuinely distinct from the frequency and cumulative-sum measures already tried, though TS_MIN(pi/at,5) will be heavily collinear with the accepted VOL(pi/at,5) leg, so the incremental information is likely modest.

Averaging two highly correlated fragility proxies that are each already being tested (one in this same batch, one in the archive) is a predictable blend whose result will fall between its components and will not identify which moment matters.

The diagnosis of the unconditional liquidation-floor result (positive FF5 alpha, wrong-signed FMB slope, negative Sharpe) is credible and the profitability gate with a centered z-score correctly parks unprofitable firms at zero rather than in a tail; the main caveat is that profitable net-cash cheapness is close to the published Graham net-net/NCAV strategy.

The construction does what the hypothesis claims (rank magnitude × signed z-score of solvency news), but GROWTH of book-to-market is dominated by the past-year price change, so the long leg is essentially 12-month losers and the test risks becoming a momentum-versus-deleveraging horse race rather than a clean price-news/fundamental-news divergence.

The min-difference construction is clever and genuinely eliminates the zero-block problem, but since IND_RANK(NEG(x)) ≈ 1 − IND_RANK(x) the expression reduces to roughly min(c, 1−L) − min(c, L), i.e. the same cheapness × loss-frequency content as Proposal 1 with the sign flipped, so it duplicates a signal in its own batch and the archive's chronic-loss trap.

critic_notes.target_name: Robust Cheapness with Deep Tail Loss
critic_notes.rationale: This is a cosmetic variant of the archived "Cheap with Deep Tail Loss" — the fragility leg is identical and only the valuation leg is replaced by an average of two already-tested multiples, which is exactly the kind of noise-reduction tweak (not a substantively different mechanism) the objective warns against.

Internally consistent and economically sensible, but it is a mechanical triple-stack of two already-evaluated archive signals (tail loss × cheapness and cash-runway × cheapness) whose product of three ranks will mostly reshuffle the same trap corner while further concentrating the extreme portfolio into a thin, unstable set.

Honest and well-motivated as a main-effect-versus-interaction diagnostic, but as a *signal* it is a direct restatement of the published distressed-growth result (Griffin–Lemmon; Campbell–Hilscher–Szilagyi) and is the exact complement of an archived expression, so it adds decomposition insight rather than a new tradable hypothesis.

The financing-of-distress channel is genuinely untouched in this archive and the sign logic is coherent, but the issuance leg is a strong standalone published anomaly (net share issuance) and GROWTH(csho) is contaminated by splits and stock dividends, so any result will need decomposition against the known issuance effect.

(act − lt)/market cap is Graham's net-current-asset-value "net-net" screen, a long-published strategy, and it is also a one-line numerator broadening of the archived (che − lt)/ME signal rather than a new mechanism.

The distance-from-own-peak transformation is a well-diagnosed repair of a specifically weak archived level signal (revenue-to-liabilities contaminated by permanent industry asset intensity), the sign and expression are internally consistent, and the scale-deterioration channel is distinct from the profitability and leverage channels already exhausted.

critic_notes.target_name: Years Spent in the Trap Corner
critic_notes.rationale: Joint-occupancy duration is a genuinely different construct from the archive's "Chronically Cheap with Heavy Claims" (which used cheapness duration times contemporaneous leverage), but the economic mechanism is the same one and the coarse 0–5 integer output plus a hard non-industry-adjusted 0.6 leverage cutoff will make portfolio extremes lumpy and sector-concentrated, so the upside over the parent is likely modest.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness Duration with Claims and Tail Loss
critic_notes.rationale: This is a mechanical blend of two existing archive signals (duration leg from "Chronically Cheap with Heavy Claims," tail-loss leg from "Cheap with Deep Tail Loss") with no new economic channel, and since leverage and cumulative tail losses are both proxies for the same solvency impairment the SUMRANK mostly double-counts rather than adding separable information.

The stated mechanism is interest-plus-depreciation fixed charges, but (ebitda − pi)/sale also absorbs special items and, critically, becomes large precisely when pi is deeply negative, so the leg is substantially a low-profitability/loss sort rather than a capital-structure-commitment measure — making it both internally inconsistent with the hypothesis and overlapping the archive's several cheap-times-unprofitability tests.

Isolating the non-current, non-funded-debt liability residual (pension, deferred tax, other accruals) is a coherent and genuinely under-tested decomposition that sits outside both the current-ratio and the leverage measures already tried, though the residual can be noisy or negative and will partly proxy capital intensity.

Growth in non-cash current assets scaled by sales is close to the well-published accruals / net-operating-asset-growth anomaly, so the distress leg is a known effect rather than a new channel, and the claimed complementarity with the accelerating working-capital-drain signal is questionable since rising receivables and inventory *increase* working capital, giving the two constructs partially opposing loadings on the same variable.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheap Level with Signed Deleveraging News
critic_notes.rationale: The diagnosis of the momentum contamination in "Cheapening Without Distress News" is correct, but the resulting expression is essentially the leverage-change half of the already-tested "Cheap with Twin Deterioration" with the profitability-change leg dropped and the sign flipped, and multiplying a strictly positive rank by a signed z-score means the extreme portfolios will be dominated by outlier delta-leverage observations in small, unstable firms.

This is a smoothed re-run of the archive's already-tested cheap×leverage trap family (Chronically Cheap with Heavy Claims, Years Spent in the Trap Corner) whose core cheap-and-distressed construct is itself the textbook value-trap/distress-risk anomaly, so a five-year moving average of the same product is a cosmetic denoising variant rather than a new mechanism.

The hypothesis explicitly claims a *union* ("exposed to either is a trap"), but SUMRANK averages the two ranks and is therefore compensatory — a firm extreme on one route and clean on the other lands mid-scale, which is the opposite of the stated logic (MAX would implement it) — and the construct is otherwise a straight blend of two already-evaluated archive signals.

The centering is mechanically correct (both extremes land in the cheap tail, sign driven by tail-loss severity, magnitude by cheapness) and the portfolio-construction diagnosis is coherent, but it remains a one-transform re-specification of the archived Cheap with Deep Tail Loss rather than a new economic channel.

The profitability *slope* is a genuinely untested moment in this archive and is economically distinguishable from level, delta, volatility, minimum and cumulative sum, though it edges close to the published fundamental-momentum/profitability-trend literature and its interaction with a value leg is the same template used a dozen times already.

Composition of near-term claims (dlc/lct) is a cleanly isolated refinancing-risk mechanism distinct from claim level, cash runway and the long-dated residual, and the expression matches the hypothesis exactly — though the reviewer should note it takes the opposite economic stance to the archived Trade-Credit-Squeezed Cheapness (which argued non-debt claims are the dangerous ones), so a weak or sign-flipped result should be interpreted against that prior.

Asset-liability maturity matching is a defensible and not-yet-tested framing, but lct/(at−act) is highly collinear with the current-ratio and act/at recovery-value tests already in the archive and its denominator is unstable for asset-light firms, so the incremental information over existing liquidity legs is likely small despite the winsorisation.

Because IND_RANK of a reciprocal is essentially one minus the original rank, this signal is mechanically the fragility main effect minus the already-archived "Cheap with Deep Tail Loss," so it adds no independent information beyond a component already tested, and "expensive plus deep loss history underperforms" is a well-worn restatement of the expensive-junk/profitability-value interaction.

The expensive-tail-plus-net-debt corner is genuinely untested in this archive and the centered second leg makes the sign logic internally consistent, though the reciprocal-rank construction means it decomposes into a net-debt main effect minus an untested cross-term, and it sits close to the published leverage-component-of-B/M result (Penman-Richardson-Tuna).

This is largely a rediscovery of the net share issuance and low-profitability anomalies dressed in a high-multiple interaction, it is again the rank-complement of an archived gen-4 signal, and the stated diagnosis ("wrong-signed slope") misreads an insignificant fmb_tstat of 1.14 as informative evidence.

A defensible falsification test of whether the gen-6 centered-fragility reversal generalises to a balance-sheet distress channel, and the expected positive sign matches the expression's direction, but structurally it is a one-input swap on an existing signal and the hypothesis runs against the well-documented distress-risk underperformance literature, so the payoff is diagnostic rather than novel alpha.

Liability growth is a close proxy for asset growth and debt issuance, both canonical published anomalies that the FF5 CMA factor will largely absorb, so the expensive-tail interaction is unlikely to deliver abnormal alpha for a reason distinct from known investment-factor effects.

The double-centered cross-term is the most conceptually interesting proposal in the batch and its sign logic is internally coherent, but the claim that it "strips both main effects" is overstated — a univariate Fama-MacBeth on a product of correlated centered variables is not orthogonal to the levels — and the long-short legs pool economically opposite firm types, which will likely produce an uninterpretable and factor-neutral spread.

This is a one-operator respecification (IND_ZSCORE→IND_RANK on the leverage leg) of the archive's best signal, and making both legs monotone ranks reintroduces the expensiveness main effect, so a strong FMB slope would largely restate the known value premium rather than validate the claimed dear-and-levered interaction.

An unweighted rank-average of two separately documented main effects (sales-to-price value and net leverage) is close to trivial as a cross-theme signal, and SUMRANK implements an average rather than the "either condition suffices" logic the hypothesis states (which would require MAX).

A coherent and correctly signed cross-tail generalization of the archive's hidden-claims channel, though it is mechanically close to (hidden-claims main effect minus the existing cheap-tail signal), so the incremental information may be modest and partly attributable to the non-current-liability level itself.

Internally consistent (the centering does keep both spread legs inside the expensive tail, and the NEG makes high values = expensive-and-untaxed = negative sign), but txt/at is a fairly direct profitability proxy, so this risks being the well-known expensive-and-unprofitable "junk growth" effect that RMW may absorb.

critic_notes.target_name: Which Risk Is Paid For Inside Value
critic_notes.rationale: The financial-versus-operating risk wedge is a genuinely novel, sign-consistent formalization of the contradiction between two prior archive results, with the caveat that it is approximately the difference of those two signals and so a strong alpha may be arithmetic rather than new information.

critic_notes.target_name: Premium Over Assets With Net Claims
critic_notes.rationale: Legs are mechanically anti-correlated (high liabilities depress book equity and hence ME/at), so the intended dear-and-encumbered corner is thinly populated and the composite largely collapses to an expensive-enterprise-value-per-asset sort, i.e., a denominator swap on the archive's best signal rather than a distinct mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Dear with Any of Three Risks
critic_notes.rationale: Adding a third arm to the gen-8 MAX union is an incremental knob-turn whose third channel (−EBITDA/LT) is largely collinear with net indebtedness, and each additional MAX arm mechanically compresses the severity leg toward its upper tail so the composite drifts back toward the expensiveness main effect (a known sales-to-price sort) rather than isolating the interaction.

The diagnosis is sound — the occupancy-count valuation leg plausibly killed the slope while producing the largest alpha — but MA(IND_RANK,5) is highly correlated with the contemporaneous rank, so this may deliver little beyond a smoothed replication of the gen-8 winner and does not truly separate "sustained" from "newly" premium firms.

The stated rationale is internally inconsistent — EBITDA/LT is a liability-scaled coverage ratio, so the claim that the signal "contains no leverage stock at all" is false and the intended clean flow-versus-encumbrance interpretation cannot be drawn — and structurally it is yet another permutation of the same MAX-union template.

This is a yardstick swap on an archive winner rather than a new mechanism, and it carries a serious construction hazard: negative-ceq firms (disproportionately the distressed names the severity leg targets) produce large negative market-to-book values that rank as "cheap," contaminating precisely the interaction being tested in a way 1% winsorization cannot repair.

A genuinely untested channel in the expensive tail with clean centered construction, though wcap/lct is essentially the current ratio and its sign is economically ambiguous among premium-valued firms, since negative working capital there often marks high-turnover, supplier-financed franchises rather than fragility.

Internally coherent and diagnostically informative about breadth versus compounding, but it changes only the aggregation operator on an existing archive signal, which is precisely the cosmetic-variant class the objective warns against; the same question could be answered with a portfolio decomposition of the existing MAX signal rather than a new evaluation slot.
